risks: "Tests from the first commit" is unsatisfiable until a runner exists: with no package.json and no lockfile, there is no `npm test` to fail. The first commit therefore has to carry the test harness, its config, and the dependency manifest together, so a genuine red-then-green cycle cannot start before scaffolding lands.

Scaffolders will meet a non-empty directory. `.git` already exists with one commit, so `create-next-app`-style tools may refuse to run in a "non-empty" directory, or skip git init and leave the repo in a half-initialized state. This is the single most likely concrete failure in the first ten minutes.

Scaffolded placeholder tests count against the completion bar. Because "nothing is finished until they pass", anything a generator emits — example tests, lint gates, typecheck steps — becomes part of the deliverable even if it was never intentionally written.

Node version mismatch. Local Node is v22.21.0 while the injected Vercel notes state Node 24 LTS is the default and Node 18 is deprecated. Pinning `engines` or depending on a framework that requires 24 will build locally and diverge on deploy, or vice versa.

Browser-based E2E tests are the natural fit for a restaurant site and the riskiest choice here: Playwright or similar needs a browser download on first run, which can fail or stall in a sandboxed environment, and there is no committed CI to make that cost visible once rather than per-developer.

Tests for a static marketing site tend to assert on copy strings. Since all content must be invented (no name, menu, hours, or address were given), every such assertion is coupled to placeholder text and will break the moment the user supplies real content — a brittle-test trap specific to this task.

Fabricated business facts ship as if real. Hours, phone number, address, prices, and especially allergen or dietary claims are public-facing representations of a real restaurant. Inventing them to make the site look complete is a content risk, not a code risk, and no amount of passing tests detects it.

Food photography has no source in the repo. Pulling remote images requires framework-level remote-host configuration and raises licensing questions; omitting images leaves a restaurant site that will not read as done regardless of test status.
